learn.hook: Imagine remembering thousands of verses perfectly, without a single book, and passing them on for thousands of years!
points: The Vedas are among the oldest texts of India, composed in an early form of Sanskrit.
There are four Vedas: the Rigveda, the Samaveda, the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is the oldest.

The Vedas were passed on by word of mouth for a very long time. Students memorised them using careful methods of chanting. UNESCO has listed the tradition of Vedic chanting as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The Rigveda has hymns to forces of nature, like Agni (fire) and Indra (linked with rain and thunder), and a famous line meaning 'Truth is one; the wise call it by many names'.
Later texts called the Upanishads discuss big questions, like 'Who am I?', through dialogues between teachers and students.

example.q: How could the Vedas survive for so long when they were not written down for centuries?
steps: Teachers recited the hymns and students repeated them exactly.
Special chanting patterns helped check that no word changed.
Each generation taught the next in the same way.
example.answer: They were memorised and passed down orally with great care.

learn.reallife: Even today, the gurukula way of learning by listening and repeating is followed in some schools of Vedic chanting.

games.title: Vedic words
pairs: the oldest of the four Vedas
texts with dialogues on big questions
passing on by word of mouth

items.text: The Vedas were first passed down by ___.

quiz.q: How many Vedas are there?
quiz.explain: The four Vedas are the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember the number of Vedas

quiz.q: Which is the oldest Veda?
quiz.explain: The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas.
quiz.mistake: Picks another Veda without knowing the order

quiz.q: In which language were the Vedas composed?
quiz.explain: The Vedas are in Vedic Sanskrit, an early form of Sanskrit.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Vedas with Buddhist texts in Pali

quiz.q: How were the Vedas passed on for many centuries?
quiz.explain: The Vedas were carried forward orally, with teachers and students chanting them carefully.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ancient texts were always written

quiz.q: Which world organisation has recognised the tradition of Vedic chanting as heritage?
quiz.explain: UNESCO recognises important cultural traditions around the world, including Vedic chanting.
quiz.mistake: Confuses UNESCO with sports or space organisations

quiz.q: What do the Upanishads mainly contain?
options: Dialogues about big questions like the self and the universe
quiz.explain: The Upanishads explore deep questions through teacher-student conversations.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what the Upanishads are about

quiz.q: The Rigvedic line 'Truth is one; the wise call it by many names' teaches us what?
options: That only one name is allowed
Respect for different ways of describing the truth
quiz.explain: The line suggests that people may describe one truth in different ways.
quiz.mistake: Takes the line to mean only one view is correct

quiz.q: What is Agni in the Rigveda?
quiz.explain: Agni means fire; many Rigvedic hymns are addressed to Agni.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Agni with a place or person

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'What are the Vedas, and how did people remember them without books?'
teach.praise: Wow! There are four Vedas, the Rigveda is the oldest, and they were passed down by careful chanting and memory for centuries!
teach.nudge: How many Vedas are there, and how were they passed on without being written?

learn.hook: A prince left his palace to find out why people suffer. Another teacher taught that even an ant's life matters. Who were they?
points: Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini (in present-day Nepal). He left his comfortable life to understand the cause of suffering.
He gained enlightenment under a pipal tree (the Bodhi tree) at Bodh Gaya in Bihar and became the Buddha, the 'awakened one'. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
The Buddha taught the Middle Path, avoiding extremes, along with the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. He taught in the language of ordinary people.
Vardhamana Mahavira was the 24th tirthankara (great teacher) of Jainism. He was born near Vaishali in Bihar.
Jainism teaches ahimsa (non-violence to all living beings), truthfulness, not owning more than needed, and anekantavada: the idea that truth has many sides.

example.q: Six friends each touch a different part of an elephant in the dark: one feels a trunk, one a tail, one a leg. Each describes 'the elephant' differently. Which Jain idea does this show?
steps: Each friend is partly right, because each knows only one part.
None of them sees the whole elephant.
The Jain idea that truth has many sides and we should listen to other views is called anekantavada.

learn.reallife: Many Jain families avoid harming even tiny insects, and Buddhist monasteries in Ladakh and Sikkim welcome visitors to learn about peace.

quiz.q: Where was Siddhartha Gautama born?
quiz.explain: The Buddha was born at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the place of birth with places of enlightenment or sermon

quiz.q: Where did the Buddha gain enlightenment?
quiz.explain: He gained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya in Bihar.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Bodh Gaya with Sarnath

quiz.q: Where did the Buddha give his first sermon?
quiz.explain: His first teaching was given at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the place of the first sermon with the place of enlightenment

quiz.q: What does the word 'Buddha' mean?
quiz.explain: Buddha means one who has woken up to the truth.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Buddha was a royal title

quiz.q: What is the Buddha's 'Middle Path'?
options: Always walking in the middle of the road
Owning as many things as possible
Avoiding extremes of too much comfort and too much hardship
quiz.explain: The Middle Path means a balanced life, avoiding both extremes.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'Middle Path' too literally

quiz.q: Mahavira was which tirthankara of Jainism?
quiz.explain: Mahavira was the 24th and last tirthankara of the present age in Jain tradition.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Mahavira founded Jainism as the first tirthankara

quiz.q: What does 'ahimsa' mean?
quiz.explain: Ahimsa means non-violence, an important teaching in Jainism and Buddhism.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of ahimsa

quiz.q: Which Jain idea says that truth has many sides?
quiz.explain: Anekantavada teaches that one thing can be seen in many ways, so we should respect other views.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up anekantavada with ahimsa

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'Who were the Buddha and Mahavira? What did they teach?'
teach.praise: Lovely! The Buddha taught the Middle Path, and Mahavira taught ahimsa and that truth has many sides. Both taught kindness!
teach.nudge: What did the Buddha teach, and what is ahimsa that Mahavira taught?

learn.hook: In ancient India, thinkers loved to debate! Instead of one answer, many 'schools of thought' grew side by side.
points: A school of thought is a group of ideas about life and the world shared by teachers and their followers.
Ancient Indian philosophy developed several schools called darshanas, such as Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta.
The Yoga school, linked with the sage Patanjali, teaches discipline of body and mind. Today, International Yoga Day is celebrated on 21 June.
Buddhism and Jainism also grew as separate schools of thought, with their own teachers and texts.
Folk and tribal traditions, like honouring nature, rivers, mountains and sacred groves of trees, are also important cultural roots. These ideas often mixed and learnt from each other.

example.q: Why do we say India's cultural roots are like the roots of a banyan tree?
steps: A banyan tree has many roots that hang down and grow into the ground.
India's culture also grew from many sources: the Vedas, Buddhism, Jainism, many darshanas and folk and tribal traditions.
All these roots support one big tree together.
example.answer: Because Indian culture grew from many different traditions that together support it.

learn.reallife: Doing yoga at school, saying 'Namaste', and villagers protecting a sacred grove near their village are all living cultural roots.

games.title: Schools of thought
items: Yoga is one of the darshanas (schools) of Indian philosophy.
Yoga is one of the classical darshanas.
International Yoga Day is celebrated on 21 June.
It is held every year on 21 June.
Ancient India had only one way of thinking.
Many schools of thought grew side by side and debated each other.
Sacred groves are patches of forest protected by local communities.
People protect them as special places and do not cut their trees.
Folk and tribal traditions are not part of India's cultural roots.
They are an important part of India's cultural roots.

games.title: Match the idea
pairs: sage linked with the Yoga school
forest patch protected by a community
discussing ideas to find the truth

quiz.q: What is a 'school of thought'?
options: A group of ideas shared by teachers and their followers
quiz.explain: A school of thought is a set of ideas, not a school building.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'school' to mean a school building

quiz.q: What were the schools of Indian philosophy called?
quiz.explain: Darshana means 'way of seeing'; the schools of philosophy were called darshanas.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up terms from other topics

quiz.q: Which sage is linked with the Yoga school of thought?
quiz.explain: The Yoga Sutras are linked with Patanjali.
quiz.mistake: Picks a person from another chapter

quiz.q: On which date is International Yoga Day celebrated?
quiz.explain: International Yoga Day is celebrated every year on 21 June.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with national holidays

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the darshanas of Indian philosophy?
quiz.explain: Nyaya, a school focused on logic and reasoning, is one of the darshanas.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up places and people with schools of thought

quiz.q: What is a sacred grove?
options: A patch of forest protected by a local community
quiz.explain: Communities protect sacred groves and avoid cutting their trees, which also saves plants and animals.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that communities protect these forests

quiz.q: The Vedanta school is mainly based on which texts?
quiz.explain: Vedanta means 'end of the Vedas' and builds on the Upanishads.
quiz.mistake: Does not link Vedanta with the Upanishads

quiz.q: What does it tell us that many schools of thought grew side by side in ancient India?
options: People were free to question, debate and think differently
There was only one teacher in the land
quiz.explain: Many schools and debates show a long tradition of questioning and discussion.
quiz.mistake: Assumes there was only one accepted view

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'Did everyone in ancient India believe the same thing?'
teach.praise: I see! Many schools of thought like Yoga, Vedanta, Buddhism and Jainism, plus folk and tribal traditions, grew side by side through debate!
teach.nudge: Was there only one way of thinking? Can you name some different schools of thought?
